definition.text: A building roof partly or fully covered with plants and a growing medium, laid over a waterproof membrane.

facts.text: Besides plants and soil, a green roof may have a root barrier, drainage layers and irrigation.
Green roofs cut energy use: they add mass and insulation against heating needs and ease the urban heat island effect by raising evapotranspiration.
A study cited by the US EPA found green roofs reduced rainwater runoff by over 75% during rainstorms.
Green roofs create habitat; even 19 stories up they can attract beneficial insects, birds, bees and butterflies.
Plants on the roof absorb carbon and store it in plant tissue and in the soil through litter and root exudates.
An extensive system can cost $108–$248/m2, an intensive one $355–$2,368/m2, and the up-front cost can be double that of a normal roof.
Covering the waterproof membrane with soil and plants shields it from sunlight and damage, which can extend a roof's life by over 200%.
Toronto approved a by-law in May 2009 requiring green roofs on residential and industrial buildings.

definition.text: Green roofs are grouped as intensive, semi-intensive or extensive according to how deep their planting medium is and how much upkeep they need.

facts.text: Extensive roofs usually carry 50–120 kg/m2 of vegetation, while intensive roofs carry 390–730 kg/m2.
Traditional roof gardens with deep soil for large plants or lawns count as intensive, because they need irrigation, feeding and other labour.

definition.text: A brown or biodiverse roof covers the flat roof of a new building with locally sourced material to replace wildlife habitat lost to development.

facts.text: Old industrial brownfield sites can be valuable ecosystems for rare plants, animals and invertebrates, but redevelopment threatens them.

definition.text: A roof that combines a blue roof's water storage with a green roof's plants, holding stormwater beneath layers of soil and vegetation.

facts.text: Its benefits include reducing stormwater runoff, reusing the stored water to irrigate the plants, and cooling the building inside.

definition.text: A green wall, living wall or vertical garden is an upright built structure deliberately covered with plants.

facts.text: Unlike a green facade, where climbing plants grow from soil at the base, a green wall holds its growing medium on the wall face itself.
French botanist Patrick Blanc is often credited with popularizing green walls, starting with a large indoor wall in Paris in 1986.
Plant surfaces cooled by transpiration stay no more than 4–5 °C above air temperature, so green walls lower building temperatures in cities.
They make good use of vertical surfaces in cities, and in dry areas their circulating water evaporates less than in flat gardens.
Living walls are credited with cleaning indoor and outdoor air; one computer model showed a wall absorbing nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter.
Green walls are often said to provide ecosystem services, and deeper substrates tend to support the most species.
They are classed by growth medium: freestanding, media-free, loose, mat and structural media.

title: Pocket forest

definition.text: A small forest made by planting many different native trees and shrubs close together, usually to restore native plants quickly in damaged places.

facts.text: Instead of passing through early growth stages, a pocket forest is planted densely with mature-stage species that race each other for sunlight.
Interest grew largely from Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki, whose 'Miyawaki forests' inspired many methods suited to different climates.
Forestry scholars say claims that Miyawaki forests grow ten times faster are unsubstantiated, and the method is called costly and unworkable for large areas.
Dense, layered pocket forests can catch embers and act as a fuel ladder, raising wildfire risk in cities.

contested_note: Forestry scholars dispute popular claims about how fast Miyawaki forests grow and question their cost and suitability.

definition.text: The care and management of individual trees and groups of trees in towns and cities to improve the urban environment.

facts.text: Urban forestry treats trees as a vital part of a city's infrastructure, and covers planting, care, protection and managing trees as a shared resource.
City trees filter air pollution, regulate local climate and store carbon dioxide.
Trees cool the urban heat island by shading pavement, helping air move and through evapotranspiration.
The United States has around 3.8 billion urban trees, with an estimated structural value of $2.4 trillion.
Heat waves kill 1,300 people a year in the United States, more than any other weather event, which gives urban shade health value.
City trees face cramped roots and canopy, poor soil, too much or too little water and light, heat, pollution and physical damage.
Urban forests bring both ecosystem services and disservices, which planners weigh beforehand.

definition.text: A street tree is any tree growing along a city street, such as between the sidewalk and the curb.

facts.text: Street trees soak up stormwater, remove air pollutants and give shade that eases the urban heat island.
Because they grow among large paved areas, street trees make up an important share of a district's tree cover.

definition.text: In town planning, urban green spaces are open areas set aside for parks and other greenery.

facts.text: The World Health Organization defines urban green space as all city land covered by vegetation of any kind.
Green spaces include plant life and water features, called blue spaces, and range from playing fields to wilder-looking land.
Their benefits fall into four groups: recreation, ecology, beauty and health.
Green spaces can clean city air, shelter wildlife and lower flood risk by draining rainwater.
Homes near urban open spaces tend to be worth more.
Visitors gain more from green spaces with more biodiversity, so quality and variety matter, not just greenness.
The Romans used the phrase 'rus in urbe', country in the city, around the first century C.E.

definition.text: The World Health Organization treats urban green space as important to people's mental and physical health.

facts.text: Green space encourages exercise and reduces air pollution, heat, traffic noise and emissions, all of which raise the risk of chronic and mental illness.
People living within 1 km of green space show lower cardiovascular disease risk.
The closer people live to parks, and the more land is parks, the fewer local treatments for anxiety and mood disorders.
Areas with many trees have markedly lower levels of pollutants such as ozone, PM10, NO2, SO2 and CO.
Plant choice matters: large tree canopies can add to asthma and allergies.
Children with more access to parks are more active, and green space is linked to better focus and working memory at school.

definition.text: The uneven sharing of parks, trees and other green space, with poorer and minority neighbourhoods often having less access.

facts.text: Neighbourhoods with more minority residents often have less park access because of past redlining and present funding choices.
Parks in minority neighbourhoods are often small, poorly kept, unsafe or unsuited to local needs.
American Forests defines tree canopy inequity as the uneven spread of city trees, with fewer in disadvantaged neighbourhoods.
As cities grow denser, more people, especially those with low incomes, live in less green surroundings.

definition.text: Biophilic design tries to connect people more closely with nature, and with nature-like design, to improve their health and well-being.

facts.text: By adding natural features such as sunlight, it offers health, environmental and economic benefits with few drawbacks.
Stephen Kellert, a pioneer of the field, built a framework of direct experience of nature, indirect experience such as images and natural materials, and experience of space and place.
In experiments, people recovered from stress faster and more fully when exposed to natural rather than urban surroundings.
Plants, trees, rain gardens and green roofs reduce hard surfaces, helping buildings and cities manage stormwater runoff.
Peter Newman estimated that biophilic design could save New York City nearly $470 million through higher worker productivity and $1.7 billion through lower crime costs.
Natural elements can cost a little more to install and maintain, but their health and environmental benefits are believed to outweigh this.
The WELL Building Standard and the Living Building Challenge are its most prominent backers in building rating systems.

definition.text: A biophilic city, in Timothy Beatley's view, is one whose residents want to take part in, protect and connect with the nature around them.

facts.text: Beatley's framework judges cities by infrastructure, governance, knowledge and behaviour, such as how many people live near a park.
He argues biophilic design helps cities adapt to the stresses of a changing climate.
Singapore, nicknamed a 'city in a garden', built a network of nature reserves, parks, connectors and tree-lined streets to bring back wildlife and reduce urban heat.

definition.text: Urban agriculture covers the growing, processing and distribution of food in towns and cities.

facts.text: It also includes raising animals, fish farming, beekeeping and horticulture in cities, and differs from peri-urban farming at the rural edge of suburbs.
Gardens and farms are its two main types; the USDA counts as a farm any place that produces and sells $1,000 or more of farm products.
Urban and peri-urban farming supplies fresh produce, jobs and income, and can improve city dwellers' food security and nutrition.
Growing food locally cuts transport energy; one study found non-local food distribution used 4 to 17 times more fuel than local and regional transport.
Urban farms can act as carbon sinks, offsetting some of the carbon build-up in places where pavement and buildings outnumber plants.
Expanding city farming often means dealing with old soil contamination, especially lead and other heavy metals.
City land is scarce and expensive, and irrigating with untreated wastewater can spread waterborne disease.

definition.text: A community garden is public space where residents grow plants for food, recreation and learning.

facts.text: In many cities small plots and rooftops are used by residents to garden.
Gardens often strengthen local social networks and give neighbourhoods a focus that builds pride.

title: Food desert
article: Urban agriculture#Health inequalities and food justice

definition.text: Low-income and minority neighbourhoods with poor access to healthy food, a pattern the USDA found well supported in 2009.

facts.text: Definitions of food deserts vary, but US studies show racial gaps in the food environment.
Urban farms that sell fresh produce at affordable prices in food deserts can narrow gaps between rich and poor neighbourhoods.

definition.text: The urban heat island effect is the way cities become noticeably warmer than the countryside around them.

facts.text: The main cause is how cities change land surfaces; waste heat from energy use is a secondary cause.
Dark materials like asphalt and concrete absorb much more sunlight and store heat, so city surfaces warm faster than rural ones.
The city–countryside difference is usually greater at night than by day and is clearest when winds are weak.
Urban areas cover about 0.5% of Earth's land but hold more than half the world's people.
Heat islands can lengthen and intensify heat waves, raise demand for air conditioning, and warm streams fed by hot stormwater.
Climate change does not cause the effect but amplifies it.
Remedies include planting trees, white or reflective cool roofs, light-coloured concrete, green infrastructure such as green roofs, and passive radiative cooling.
Luke Howard first described it in the 1810s, reporting that central London was 2.1 °C warmer at night than the surrounding countryside.

title: Urban heat inequity
article: Urban heat island#Aspects of social inequality

definition.text: Urban heat inequity, or thermal inequity, is the uneven spread of heat across a city that hits some communities harder than others.

facts.text: Unequal heat stress often tracks race, ethnicity, income, education and age.
In most US cities, people of color are more likely than white residents to live in the hottest areas.
Past redlining shaped land use and still leaves vegetation, and so heat, unevenly shared.
Top-floor homes, dark roofs, poor insulation and lack of affordable air conditioning make the heat worse for low-income households.

title: Cool roof
article: Urban heat island#Cool roofs and light-coloured concrete

definition.text: Painting rooftops white has become a common way to reduce the heat island effect.

facts.text: Cities have many dark surfaces that absorb the sun's heat and lower the city's albedo, or reflectiveness.
A passive daytime radiative cooling roof can double the energy savings of a white roof, most of all in hot, dry cities such as Phoenix and Las Vegas.

definition.text: An urban or city park is a park or garden in a town or suburb that gives residents and visitors green space and places to relax and play.

facts.text: Urban parks are usually designed landscapes rather than land left natural, and are mostly run by local government.
Trees are picked for beauty and shade, with growing focus on reducing the urban heat island.
A 2025 satellite study of 2,083 parks found well-treed parks were on average 3.4°C cooler in summer daytime than surrounding urban areas.
Early purpose-built public parks included Princes Park in Liverpool, opened in 1843, and Birkenhead Park, which Olmsted visited in 1850.
As city land prices rose, most new US urban parks since the 1960s have been small pocket parks.
The UK has about 27,000 public parks with around 2.6 billion visits a year, but councils have no legal duty to fund them.

definition.text: Park space is split into active recreation areas, built up for sports and play, and passive recreation areas that keep open space and natural habitat.

facts.text: Active recreation such as team sports needs a lot of space, management, maintenance and money.
Passive recreation, such as trails, benches and picnic areas, needs little management and can be provided very cheaply.

definition.text: A linear park is a park much longer than it is wide.

facts.text: A typical example is an old railway line turned into a rail trail or greenway, with the tracks removed and plants allowed back.
New York's High Line is a North American example.

definition.text: A blue roof is designed to store rainwater for a while and then release it slowly.

facts.text: They are built on flat roofs in cities where too few permeable surfaces let rain soak into the ground, raising flood risk.
By easing the load on storm sewers, they help stop combined sewers overflowing untreated wastewater into rivers and coasts.
Active blue roofs control drainage with valves, while passive ones slow water by lengthening its path to the drain.
In dry climates they serve as a water-saving tool by harvesting roof rainfall.

title: Green belt

definition.text: A green belt is a planning policy and zone that keeps mostly undeveloped, wild or farmed land around or beside towns and cities.

facts.text: It works like an invisible border that blocks building and lets wildlife return; greenways and green wedges are similar but run through a city as strips.
Stated aims include protecting natural areas, improving city air, giving townspeople access to the countryside and keeping rural communities from being swallowed by suburbs.
Octavia Hill first used the term about London's growth in 1875, and the UK pioneered green belt policy.
England's fourteen green belt areas cover 16,716 km2, or 12.4% of England.
Critics such as the Institute of Economic Affairs say green belts stop new housing meeting demand and so push up house prices.
Because a green belt has an outer edge, building can leap over it, which may increase urban sprawl and lengthen commutes.
Defenders point to peri-urban farming in green belts, which stores carbon, reduces urban heat and provides habitat.

contested_note: Critics argue green belts raise house prices and spread sprawl, while supporters stress their environmental and farming benefits.

definition.text: Green urbanism is the practice of building communities that are good for both people and the environment.

facts.text: Timothy Beatley describes it as shaping more sustainable places and lifestyles that use less of the world's resources.
Its principles start from the view that urbanization is a key driver of carbon emissions, resource depletion and environmental damage, and aim for zero fossil fuels, zero waste and zero emissions.
In 1989 ecologist H.T. Odum called cities 'parasites' that make no food and clean no air but only consume.
It is interdisciplinary, drawing on planners, ecologists, engineers, economists, psychologists and others.

definition.text: Urban ecology is the scientific study of how living things relate to each other and to their surroundings in cities.

facts.text: Urban environments are dominated by dense buildings and paved surfaces, which create a distinctive landscape.
Its goal is a balance between human culture and the natural environment; ecologists turned to cities largely from the 1970s.
Researchers use chemical tests, temperature records and heat maps, remote sensing and long-term ecological research sites.
Urban demand for chemicals disturbs biogeochemical cycles, causing acid rain, eutrophication and global warming, while paving stops nutrients returning to soil.
Green infrastructure can make urban areas better homes for wildlife.
Many effects of urbanization are still poorly understood because the field is young.

definition.text: An urban forest is a forest or grove of trees growing inside a city, town or suburb.

facts.text: Unlike a forest park, an urban forest often lacks amenities such as toilets, paved paths or clear borders; its care is called urban forestry.
Urban forests moderate local climate, slow wind and stormwater, filter air, and help cool the urban heat island.
Models suggest 100 million trees in US cities could cut annual energy use by 30 billion kWh, saving $2 billion and 9 million tons of power plant CO2 a year.
A 40-year study in Tucson calculated $600,000 saved in stormwater treatment costs thanks to urban trees.
A Finnish study found property values rose 4.9% for each kilometre closer to a forest; a front-yard tree may add $7,130 to a home's price.
In Philadelphia, residents below the poverty line near 'greened' vacant lots reported a 68% fall in feelings of depression.
Johannesburg, on naturally treeless grassland, reportedly has 10 million planted trees and is often called the largest man-made urban forest.

conflicts.text: Another source claims the property value increase near forests can be as high as 20%.
conflicts.note: Different studies of the same premium; the 4.9% figure is per kilometre closer in Finland.

definition.text: Urban resilience is a city's or urban community's ability to withstand, recover from or adapt to human-made and natural disasters.

facts.text: It covers physical infrastructure as well as social, health and economic systems.
Research has focused on three main threats: climate change, natural disasters and terrorism.
A study of 616 cities, home to 1.7 billion people, found floods endanger more city residents than any other natural hazard, followed by earthquakes and storms.
Greening is among the most often cited heat strategies: covering surfaces with plants reduces heat-absorbing material and shades concrete and asphalt.
Replacing hard surfaces with greenery lets soil and plants soak up excess rain, and deeper green roof soils absorb more.
Older people make up most heat-related deaths in cities, and social isolation adds to their risk.
Building resilience means investing in options that work across uncertain futures, since risk can never be fully removed.

definition.text: Urban rewilding is a form of rewilding that tries to bring working ecosystems, from plants to animals, into cities.

facts.text: There are four types: urban greening, corridors, small-scale projects under 50 hectares and large-scale projects over 50 hectares.
Corridors such as restored waterways or green paths link habitats so city animals can move freely.
Benefits include cleaner air, stored carbon, more pollination, fertile soil, clean water and lower stress.
Projects are costly and carry an opportunity cost, since owners could use the land for more profitable purposes.

title: Urban biodiversity

definition.text: The variety of plant and animal life found in cities, which planners can sustain by enlarging green areas and linking them with green corridors.

facts.text: Increasing green areas and building a network of green corridors is a successful way to keep urban biodiversity high.
In temperate countries, urbanization often adds non-native species while cutting native ones, lowering overall species richness.
Cities reduce diversity by removing and fragmenting habitat and by making once-distinct communities more alike.
Green roofs, tree inventories, planting of hardy species and protecting parks and woodlots can all support urban biodiversity.
Safe movement paths for wildlife, better habitat and fewer human threats help sustain it.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; also draws on Urban ecology#Biodiversity and urbanization.
